rv.q: This is a production that has magic to spare.
Indhu Rubasingham’s wonderful production of The Father and the Assassin puts on stage an important piece of history, an arresting personal story and a vital, distinctive theatrical language.
It’s exhilarating to see such big, bold political history commanding the National Theatre’s largest stage.

Epic in scope but grounded in the parallel personal journeys of these two complex figures, The Father and the Assassin successfully weaves a thorny mass of contentious history and factional politics into a tight and accessible drama.
Indhu Rubasingham's two-and-a-half hour jaunt through half a century of Indian political history is always entertaining.

No question, this is a fascinating, important evening, with valuably shaming moments of British imperial brutality referenced en route and a topical sting in the tale about rising intolerance (there are statues now to Godse).
The play is heavy on exposition but oddly short on dramatic substance.
Shubham Saraf imparts just about enough craziness into Godse to save the show from becoming an apologia for Islamophobia.
Despite its playful flourishes and some eye-catching set pieces, it’s a stolid evening.
It is a star-making performance in an ideal production of a play that turns a foregone conclusion into a dynamic evening of inevitable history that plays as a succession of surprises.
The pure confidence of that opening is characteristic of this superb production of Anupama Chandrasekhar's terrific, stirring new play.
It makes bold and invigorating theatre that is discreetly underlined by Siddhartha Khosla’s music which rises to a dramatic crescendo when partition is presented.
It is a fitting setting for colourful, ambitious, fast-paced storytelling.
Shubham Saraf, a hugely charismatic performer, brings levity and an impish quirkiness to the role of the smirking killer.
With a company of 19, some crowd scenes are thrilling, but others are confusing.
This remains a highly entertaining and enlightening evening that succeeds in balancing epic sweep with emotional intimacy.
I subtract two stars however for historical incompleteness and want of ambition.

cn.t: Critics praise Chandrasekhar's bold, provocative play about Gandhi's assassin as theatrically ambitious and timely, with Saraf's charismatic performance earning widespread acclaim, though some find the playful tone jarring for such weighty subject matter.
